title: Executive Functions Profiles in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Associations with Behavioral and Emotional Difficulties
abstract: Children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) often exhibit deficits in executive functions (EFs), with cognitive flexibility being one of the primary functions affected in ASD. Numerous studies have investigated how these deficits are associated with the socio-emotional difficulties exhibited by children with ASD. In our study, we investigated EF deficits, behavioral flexibility, and how they are associated with behavioral and socio-emotional difficulties. Our sample included 59 children aged 6–14 years (SD = 2.09; M = 9.85) diagnosed with ASD. Our results showed that EF difficulties in inhibition and regulation correlated most strongly with externalizing and hyperactive behaviors, whereas flexibility difficulties, particularly transitions and generativity, correlated more strongly with internalizing problems, peer difficulties, and reduced prosocial behavior. Regression analyses indicated that flexibility dimensions jointly predicted prosocial behavior, peer problems, and internalizing problems, with transition difficulties as the most consistent independent predictor; age was not associated with flexibility difficulties. These findings indicate that executive and flexibility-related difficulties are differentially linked to distinct behavioral and socio-emotional outcomes in ASD, with implications for targeted intervention. Limitations include the correlational design, informant-based measures, and the absence of a typically developing comparison group.
